lesson.title: The Hole You Can Patch: Removable Discontinuity
lesson.summary: A removable discontinuity is a point where the limit exists perfectly well but the function value is missing or wrong, meaning a single, correct redefinition erases the break entirely.
lesson.body:
A discontinuity at c is called removable when lim(x to c) f(x) exists as a finite number, but either f(c) is undefined or f(c) does not equal that limit. The word removable is a promise: because the limit already exists and already tells you exactly what value would make everything work, you can remove the discontinuity by defining, or redefining, f(c) to equal that limit. Nothing about the function's behavior near c needs to change at all, since it was already heading toward a single, well-defined value. Only the single point c itself needs a patch.

Removable discontinuities show up constantly in algebraic quotients that produce the indeterminate form 0/0 at a particular input. When both the numerator and denominator of a rational expression vanish at x = c, direct substitution gives 0/0, which reveals nothing on its own, but it also signals that (x - c) is a common factor of both the top and the bottom. Cancel that shared factor algebraically, and the resulting simplified expression usually has a well-behaved limit at x = c, even though the original, unsimplified formula is undefined there.

Worked example: let f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3). Substituting x = 3 gives (9 - 9)/(3 - 3) = 0/0, the indeterminate form, so f(3) is undefined and direct substitution tells us nothing yet. Factor the numerator as a difference of squares: x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3). For x not equal to 3, f(x) = (x - 3)(x + 3)/(x - 3) = x + 3. So lim(x to 3) f(x) = lim(x to 3) (x + 3) = 6. The limit exists and equals 6, while f(3) is undefined, so this is a removable discontinuity at x = 3. Defining a new value of 6 there removes it completely.

A removable discontinuity does not always come from a missing value. Let g(x) = x for every x except x = 2, where instead g(2) = 9. Here lim(x to 2) g(x) = 2, since g agrees with the simple line y = x at every point near 2 other than 2 itself, but g(2) = 9 does not match that limit. The discontinuity is still removable, since redefining g(2) to be 2 instead of 9 fixes the mismatch and makes g continuous at that point, exactly as in the missing-value case, just starting from a wrong value rather than no value.

The defining feature that separates a removable discontinuity from every other kind is that the limit exists in the first place. If the one-sided limits disagree, or if either one runs off to infinity, or if the function oscillates without settling anywhere, there is no single value that a patch could supply, and the discontinuity is not removable. That existence of a genuine limiting value is exactly what the next concept, continuous extension, turns into a formal procedure for building a new, fully continuous function out of one that merely has a hole in it.

It is also worth remembering that the algebra used to find the patch value, factoring, canceling, or rationalizing, is only a tool for computing the limit. The removable discontinuity itself is defined purely in terms of that limit existing and disagreeing with, or replacing, the function value at c. Whenever a 0/0 form appears from direct substitution in a rational or radical expression, that is a strong hint that a removable discontinuity, rather than some other kind, is what you are dealing with, since a shared factor is very often waiting to be canceled out.
